lead: Unit 3 is about strings and the built-in collections: list, tuple, dictionary and set. After it you can slice and clean any text, choose the right collection for a job, avoid the aliasing bug that copies nothing, and search a sorted list in about log₂ n steps instead of n.
about: Unit 3 turns the single string of Unit 1 into the four built-in collections every Python program uses. Chapter 3.1 fixes the rules of strings: literals, indexing, slicing and the common methods. Chapter 3.2 adds formatting, comparison, splitting and stripping. Chapter 3.3 moves to lists and to the idea that a name holds a reference, so aliasing and copying must be understood. Chapter 3.4 compresses list building into one line. Chapter 3.5 gives the immutable tuple, and 3.6 and 3.7 give the two hash-based collections, dictionary and set. Chapter 3.8 uses the two ends of a list as stack and queue, and 3.9 closes with searching and sorting, where binary search depends on the sorted order that 3.9 itself explains.

chapters.idea: A string is an immutable sequence of characters, so it can be indexed and sliced but never edited in place.
chapters.depth: String literals with single, double and triple quotes; escape sequences \n, \t, \\, \' and raw strings r'...'. A string is a sequence of characters: len(), positive and negative indexing, IndexError when the index is out of range. Slicing s[start:stop:step] with all defaults left out, negative steps, s[::-1]; a slice always makes a new string. Operators +, *, in and not in; ordering of single characters through ord() and chr(). Methods: upper, lower, title, capitalize, swapcase, find, rfind, index, count, replace, startswith, endswith, isdigit, isalpha, isalnum, isspace, join. Say plainly that every method returns a new string. Some syllabi call looping over characters 'string traversal'.

figure.title: s = 'python': slicing and reversing
figure.caption: The characters at indexes 1, 2 and 3 make s[1:4]; the pointer at index 4 shows where the slice stops, and the second row is the same string read backwards.
figure.aria: A six-cell row holds the characters of 'python' with their indexes, three cells shaded for the slice, and a second row holds the reversed string.

chapters.example: For s = 'python' give s[0], s[-1], s[1:4], s[::-1], s.upper(), s.replace('p', 'P'), s.find('t') and len(s), then state the value of s afterwards. Answers: 'p'; 'n'; 'yth'; 'nohtyp'; 'PYTHON'; 'Python'; 2; 6; s is still 'python', because every method returned a new string.
chapters.trap: A slice stops before its second index, so s[1:4] has three characters and not four; and s.upper() does not change s, which is the usual wrong answer to 'what is s now'.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: variables, data types, operators and print().
chapters.leave: split, strip, formatting and comparison go to 3.2; methods that return lists feed 3.4; regular expressions go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Formatting turns values into text, comparison orders that text by code point, and split, strip and join move between one string and many.
chapters.depth: Three formatting styles: the % operator, str.format() and f-strings, with width, alignment, precision and thousands separator, as in {0:.2f}, {:>8} and {:,}. Comparison: == compares characters, is compares identity; ordering is lexicographic by Unicode code point, so uppercase letters sort before lowercase ones, ord('A') = 65 and ord('a') = 97; case-insensitive compare with lower() or casefold(). Splitting: split() with no argument splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty pieces, split(sep, maxsplit), rsplit, splitlines. Joining: sep.join(list) needs every element to be a string, otherwise TypeError. Stripping: strip, lstrip, rstrip with an optional set of characters.

figure.title: one string to many and back
figure.caption: Splitting turns one string into three pieces, stripping cleans each piece, and joining puts them back with new separators.
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow from a raw comma-separated string through split and strip to a join that produces one clean string.

chapters.example: s = '  red, green ,blue  '. Find s.strip(), s.strip().split(','), the same list after stripping each piece in a for loop, and ' - '.join(parts). Then format 1234.5 as f'₹{1234.5:,.2f}'. Answers: 'red, green ,blue'; ['red', ' green ', 'blue']; ['red', 'green', 'blue']; 'red - green - blue'; '₹1,234.50'. Also 'Apple' < 'apple' is True because ord('A') = 65 is smaller than ord('a') = 97.
chapters.trap: strip('ab') removes any of the characters a and b from the two ends, not the word 'ab'; and split() with no argument drops empty pieces while split(' ') keeps them.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for indexing, slicing and the base methods.
chapters.leave: f-string debugging with = and regular expressions go to Unit 5; building the cleaned list with a comprehension goes to 3.4; sorting rules for strings go to 3.9.

chapters.idea: A list is a mutable ordered sequence, and a variable name holds a reference to the list, so two names can point at one object.
chapters.depth: List literals with any mix of types, nested lists and a[i][j]. Operators +, *, in, == and element-by-element comparison. Methods append, extend, insert, remove, pop, clear, index, count, sort, reverse, copy, and the del statement; sorted() returns a new list while sort() changes the list in place. Mutability: b = a is aliasing, a[:] and a.copy() are shallow copies; id() and is show the difference, and a change through one name is visible through the other. Some syllabi call aliasing a 'reference copy' and shallow copying a 'surface copy'.

figure.caption: Names a and b reach the same list object, so a change through a shows through b; c was made with a slice and owns its own list.
figure.aria: Two names a and b point to one list object while c points, with a dashed arrow, to a separate copy.

chapters.example: a = [10, 20, 30]; b = a; c = a[:]; a.append(40); a[1] = 99. Give a, b, c, id(a) == id(b) and id(a) == id(c). Answers: a = [10, 99, 30, 40]; b = [10, 99, 30, 40] because b is the same object; c = [10, 20, 30] because the slice copied the list before the changes; True; False.
chapters.trap: b = a copies the reference, not the list; a[:] and a.copy() are only one level deep, so n.copy()[0].append(5) also changes n.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for indexing and slicing; Unit 1 for assignment, id() and operators.
chapters.leave: comprehension goes to 3.4; tuples to 3.5; stack and queue uses to 3.8; searching and sorting to 3.9.

chapters.idea: A list comprehension builds a new list from a loop, an optional filter and an expression, all written in one line.
chapters.depth: [expr for item in iterable] and the filtered form [expr for item in iterable if cond]. The order is expression, then for clauses, then if clauses; the expression itself may hold if-else. Write the equivalent for loop beside each comprehension and show they give the same list. Nested for clauses run like nested loops, left to right. Iterate over range, a string, or dict.items(). The result is always a new list, never a change to the old one. Keep to one or two clauses for readability. In one line: set and dict comprehensions use the same pattern (3.7 and 3.6) and generator expressions belong to Unit 4.

figure.title: x * x for even x in 1 to 6
figure.caption: The numbers 1 to 6 pass through the loop and the even filter; only 2, 4 and 6 reach the expression and become 4, 16 and 36.
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow from the numbers 1 to 6 through a for clause and an even-number filter to the squared values 4, 16 and 36.

chapters.example: Give the output of [x*x for x in range(1, 7) if x % 2 == 0], of [x if x > 0 else 0 for x in [-2, 3, -1, 5]] and of [i + j for i in range(1, 3) for j in range(1, 3)]. Answers: [4, 16, 36]; [0, 3, 0, 5]; [2, 3, 3, 4].
chapters.trap: The if filter comes after the for clause, and an if-else must always carry its else; writing 'if x % 2 == 0 for x in ...' is a syntax error.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 lists; Unit 2 for loops and range().
chapters.leave: generators and yield go to Unit 4; set and dict comprehensions to 3.7 and 3.6; map and filter to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A tuple is an immutable ordered sequence, so it is safe to share and, when all items are hashable, it can be a dictionary key.
chapters.depth: Creating tuples: (), (1,), 1, 2, 3 without brackets, and tuple(iterable). The comma makes the tuple, not the brackets. Indexing and slicing like a list, plus len, count, index, in, +, *, min, max and sum; sorted(t) returns a list, not a tuple. Packing and unpacking a, b = t, the swap a, b = b, a, nested tuples, and comparison element by element. Immutability: t[0] = 5 raises TypeError. A tuple is hashable when every item is, so it can be a key in a dictionary (3.6). Only a few universities teach namedtuple; it is left out here.

figure.title: t = (10, 20, 30) and one more element
figure.caption: The second element cannot be assigned a new value; adding 40 builds a different, longer tuple instead of changing t.
figure.aria: A three-item tuple with its second element marked as not assignable, and a second row showing the longer tuple produced by adding 40.

chapters.example: t = (10, 20, 30). Give t[1], t[1:3], len(t), t + (40,), t * 2, and unpack a, b, c = t. Then say what t[1] = 99 does and what types (5) and (5,) have. Answers: 20; (20, 30); 3; (10, 20, 30, 40); (10, 20, 30, 10, 20, 30); a = 10, b = 20, c = 30; TypeError because tuples do not support item assignment; (5) is an int and (5,) is a tuple.
chapters.trap: A one-item tuple needs the comma: (5) is an int, and t + (40) raises TypeError because (40) is plain 40.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 for sequence operators, slicing and shallow copying.
chapters.leave: namedtuple goes to a later unit; tuple keys are used in 3.6; returning several values from a function goes to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A dictionary maps unique hashable keys to values, and getting, adding, replacing and deleting all work by key.
chapters.depth: Dictionary literals {key: value}, the dict() constructor, and dict built from a list of pairs. Access with d[k], KeyError on a missing key, get(k) and get(k, default); the in test looks only at keys. Adding and replacing: d[new] = v and d[old] = v2. Removing: del d[k], pop(k), pop(k, default), popitem(), clear(). Views keys(), values() and items(), looping with d.items(), update(), len(). Copying with d.copy() versus aliasing, as in 3.3. Insertion order is kept. Keys must be hashable, so int, str and tuples of immutables are allowed and lists are not. Some syllabi call these 'mapping operations'. One short dictionary comprehension example.

figure.title: keys map to values
figure.caption: Looking up the shaded key 'b' returns 20 from the row below; assigning to a key that is not there adds a whole new column.
figure.aria: A two-row table with keys 'a', 'b' and 'c' above the values 10, 20 and 30, with the b column shaded.

chapters.example: Start with d = {'a': 10, 'b': 20}. Show d['a'], d['c'] = 30, d['a'] = 99, d.get('z'), d.pop('b') and len(d), and say what d['z'] does. Answers: 10; d becomes {'a': 10, 'b': 20, 'c': 30}; d becomes {'a': 99, 'b': 20, 'c': 30}; None; 20 and d becomes {'a': 99, 'c': 30}; 2; d['z'] raises KeyError.
chapters.trap: d['z'] raises KeyError but d.get('z') returns None, and 'a' in d tests the keys, never the values.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for string keys; 3.5 for tuple keys; 3.3 for views, copying and aliasing.
chapters.leave: CSV and JSON files with the csv module go to Unit 5; counting loops become a comprehension in 3.4; Pandas Series in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A set is an unordered collection of unique hashable items that supports union, intersection, difference and subset tests.
chapters.depth: Creating sets with {1, 2, 3}, the empty set with set() because {} is an empty dict, and set(iterable) which drops duplicates. No indexing and no slicing; iteration order is not guaranteed. add, remove (KeyError if absent), discard, pop, clear, len, and a fast in test. Operations union |, intersection &, difference -, symmetric difference ^, plus the method forms; the comparison operators <= for subset and >= for superset, and isdisjoint. Only hashable items can go in. frozenset is the immutable version and can be a dictionary key or an item of another set; only a few universities ask for it in depth.

figure.caption: The overlap holds 3 and 4, so A & B = {3, 4}; everything shown together is A | B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.
figure.aria: Two overlapping circles, A holding 1, 2, 3 and 4 and B holding 3, 4 and 5, with 3 and 4 in the overlap.

chapters.example: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. Give A | B, A & B, A - B, B - A, A ^ B and A <= B. Then turn the list [3, 1, 3, 2, 1] into a set. Answers: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; {3, 4}; {1, 2}; {5}; {1, 2, 5}; False, because 1 and 2 are not in B; {1, 2, 3}, and turning it back into a list gives an order that depends on hashing, not on position in the original list.
chapters.trap: {} creates an empty dictionary, so the empty set must be written set(); and remove() raises KeyError while discard() stays silent.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 and 3.5 for which types are hashable and which are not.
chapters.leave: frozenset in depth goes later; dictionary keys behave like a set and are covered in 3.6; abstract data structures go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Because a list grows and shrinks at either end, append with pop gives a stack and append with pop(0) gives a queue.
chapters.depth: Stack, last in first out: push with append, pop with pop(), peek with s[-1], empty check with len(s) == 0. Queue, first in first out: enqueue with append, dequeue with pop(0), which shifts every remaining item and so costs O(n); collections.deque with append and popleft is O(1) at both ends and only a few universities require it. Applications: undo, the browser back button, bracket matching, the function call stack; a printer queue, a ticket queue, breadth-first search. Popping an empty list raises IndexError. Python's list already has every method the two abstract data types need, so no class is needed here; Unit 4 shows the class version.

figure.title: a list used as a stack
figure.caption: Push adds at the right end and pop takes from the same end, so the last item pushed is the first one out.
figure.aria: A stack row 10, 20, 30 with a pointer on the top item, and after one pop a row 10, 20 with the pointer moved one cell left.

chapters.example: Build a stack s = [] with s.append(10), s.append(20), s.append(30), then s.pop() and s[-1]. Build a queue q = [] with q.append('A'), q.append('B'), q.append('C'), then q.pop(0). Answers: pop() returns 30 and s = [10, 20]; s[-1] is 20; q.pop(0) returns 'A' and q = ['B', 'C'].
chapters.trap: pop() takes from the end (last in first out) and pop(0) takes from the front (first in first out) but costs O(n) on a long list; both raise IndexError when the list is empty.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 for append, pop and the other list methods.
chapters.leave: deque in detail and breadth-first search go to Unit 6; the function call stack goes to Unit 2 recursion; writing a Stack class goes to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Linear search checks every item in order, while binary search halves a sorted list at each step.
chapters.depth: Linear search: compare each element in turn with a for loop, return the index or -1; works on any list; one comparison in the best case, n in the worst, so O(n). Binary search: the list must be sorted; keep low, high and mid = (low + high) // 2, compare, and halve; O(log₂ n) comparisons, so 1,000 items need about 10 steps. Write both with a while loop and with a for loop, and count comparisons. Sorting: list.sort() in place and sorted() returning a new list, with key and reverse; one exchange (bubble) sort and one selection sort worked by hand; Python's built-in sort is Timsort, a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort. End with a best, average and worst case table. Some syllabi call linear search 'sequential search'.

figure.title: binary search for 27
figure.caption: 21 is smaller than 27, so the left half is dropped; 33 is larger, so the right half is dropped; the next middle is 27 itself, found in three comparisons.
figure.aria: Three rows over the same seven sorted numbers, each shading the middle element checked and greying out the half that is discarded.

chapters.example: Search 27 in L = [3, 9, 14, 21, 27, 33, 40]. Linear search compares 3, 9, 14, 21 and 27, so 5 comparisons, index 4. Binary search: low 0, high 6, mid 3 gives 21 < 27; low 4, mid 5 gives 33 > 27; high 4, mid 4 gives 27, so 3 comparisons, index 4. For 1,000 items linear search needs up to 1,000 comparisons and binary search about 10, since log₂ 1000 is about 10.
chapters.trap: Binary search on an unsorted list gives a wrong answer without any error; and setting low = mid instead of mid + 1 makes the loop run forever.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 lists; 3.4 for building lists quickly; Unit 2 for while and for loops.
chapters.leave: complexity notation in depth and merge or quick sort go to later; sorting records by a field goes to Unit 6 data handling.
